title: Reported statement: said that
plainEnglish: It relays what someone else said as a statement, like English said that.
whenToUse: Use it to pass on what a person told you, in texts, gossip, or office updates. Example: 팀장님이 회의가 30분 늦어진다고 했어요 (The team lead said the meeting is pushed back 30 minutes).
attachmentRule: For a present-tense verb add -ㄴ다고 after a vowel stem (가다→간다고) and -는다고 after a consonant stem (먹다→먹는다고). Adjectives and 있다/없다 just add -다고 (춥다→춥다고, 재미있다→재미있다고). Past tense uses -았/었다고 (갔다고, 먹었다고). A noun takes -(이)라고 (학생이라고, 친구라고). 하다 is usually said as 했어요 (said) or 한다고/하더라고 in retelling.
contrastWith: -다고 하다 reports a plain statement, while -냐고 하다 reports a question and -(으)라고 하다 reports a command, so match the ending to the kind of sentence you are relaying.

examples.en: My girlfriend said she is a bit tired today.
The team lead said the meeting will be 30 minutes late.

examples.ko: 집주인이 다음 달부터 월세 올린다고 했어요.
examples.en: The landlord said he will raise the rent starting next month.

examples.ko: 걔가 어제 그 카페 진짜 맛있었다고 했어.
examples.en: She said that cafe was really good yesterday.

commonMistakes: Using the plain polite form before -다고, like 가요고 하다; you must use the plain stem form, so it is 간다고 해요, not 가요고 해요.
Forgetting the verb vs adjective split: verbs need -ㄴ다고/-는다고 (먹는다고), but adjectives just take -다고 (춥다고), so 춥는다고 is wrong.

practiceItems.prompt: My friend said he is coming tomorrow.
She said the food was delicious. (past)
The boss said he is busy.

studyOrder: Decide if the relayed sentence is a verb, adjective, or noun
Verbs: add -ㄴ다고 after a vowel, -는다고 after a consonant
Adjectives and 있다/없다: just add -다고; nouns add -(이)라고
Finish with 하다, usually 했어요 to mean someone said
beginnerExplanation: V-다고 하다 is how Korean relays what someone said, the way English uses said that. The tricky part is the front ending, because present-tense verbs do not keep the polite -요 form; instead they switch to the plain shape, so 가다 becomes 간다고 and 먹다 becomes 먹는다고. Adjectives are easier and simply add -다고, as in 피곤하다고 (said she is tired), and past tense for everything is -았/었다고 (맛있었다고). You will hear this constantly in real life: 팀장님이 회의 늦는다고 했어요 passes on the boss's message, and 친구가 내일 온다고 했어요 reports a friend's plan. The number one beginner slip is gluing -다고 onto the polite form, so remember it is 간다고 해요, never 가요고 해요.

title: Reported question: asked whether
plainEnglish: It relays a question that someone else asked, like English asked whether or asked if.
whenToUse: Use it to pass on a question another person asked you or someone else. Example: 친구가 주말에 시간 있냐고 물어봤어요 (My friend asked if I have time this weekend).
attachmentRule: In everyday speech add -냐고 to the plain stem of verbs, adjectives, and 있다/없다 alike (가냐고, 먹냐고, 바쁘냐고, 있냐고). Past tense uses -았/었냐고 (갔냐고, 먹었냐고). A noun takes -(이)냐고 (학생이냐고, 누구냐고). The reporting verb is usually 물어봤어요 (asked) or 했어요. The fuller written forms 가느냐고/먹느냐고 also exist but sound stiff in speech.
contrastWith: -냐고 하다 reports a question, while -다고 하다 reports a plain statement; if the original sentence had a question mark, use -냐고.

examples.en: My friend asked if I have time this weekend.

examples.ko: 면접관이 왜 우리 회사에 지원했냐고 물어봤어요.
examples.en: The interviewer asked why I applied to our company.
The girl I'm into asked me if I have a girlfriend.
My mom asked whether I had eaten.

commonMistakes: Using -다고 for a relayed question, like 시간 있다고 물어봤어요; a reported question needs -냐고, so it is 시간 있냐고 물어봤어요.
Keeping the polite -요 before -냐고, like 가요냐고; attach -냐고 to the plain stem, so 가냐고, not 가요냐고.

practiceItems.prompt: My friend asked if I'm coming.
He asked if it was expensive. (past)
She asked who that person is.

studyOrder: Confirm the original sentence was a question
Add -냐고 to the plain stem of the verb or adjective
Use -았/었냐고 for past and -(이)냐고 for nouns
Finish with 물어봤어요 or 했어요 to mean someone asked
beginnerExplanation: V-냐고 하다 relays a question that someone asked, matching English asked if or asked whether. The big convenience is that modern spoken Korean uses one ending, -냐고, for verbs, adjectives, and 있다/없다 alike, so you say 가냐고 (asked if I go), 바쁘냐고 (asked if I'm busy), and 시간 있냐고 (asked if I have time) all the same way. Past questions use -았/었냐고, as in 밥 먹었냐고 했어요 (asked whether I ate). The reporting verb is most naturally 물어봤어요, literally tried asking, which sounds warm and conversational. Beginners often reuse -다고 here, but that ending is only for statements; if the original had a question mark, switch to -냐고, so 여자친구 있냐고 물어봤어, not 있다고.

title: Worried that / afraid that
plainEnglish: It says you do something because you are worried or afraid that an unwanted thing might happen.
whenToUse: Use it to give an anxious reason for an action. Example: 지각할까 봐 택시 탔어요 (I took a taxi because I was worried I'd be late).
attachmentRule: Add -ㄹ까 봐 to a vowel-ending stem (가다→갈까 봐, 오다→올까 봐) and -을까 봐 to a consonant-ending stem (늦다→늦을까 봐, 먹다→먹을까 봐). For a worry about something already past, use -았/었을까 봐 (실수했을까 봐). The main clause is your reaction, often ending in a past action you took. The full form 봐요 is more polite; 봐 is casual.
contrastWith: -(으)ㄹ까 봐 gives a worried reason, while -(으)니까 gives a neutral, factual reason; use -(으)ㄹ까 봐 only when there is real worry or fear about a bad outcome.

examples.ko: 길 막힐까 봐 한 시간 일찍 나왔어요.
examples.en: I left an hour early because I was worried traffic would be bad.
I'm so nervous because I'm afraid I'll fail the interview.
I kept checking because I was afraid my message had been ignored.
I packed an umbrella in case it rains.

commonMistakes: Using it for a neutral reason instead of a worry, like 배고플까 봐 먹어요 to just mean because I'm hungry; use -(으)니까 unless there is real worry.
Forgetting the consonant linker, like saying 늦까 봐 instead of the correct 늦을까 봐.

practiceItems.prompt: I left early because I was worried I'd be late.
I packed extra because I was afraid it wouldn't be enough.

studyOrder: Identify the bad outcome you are worried about
Add -ㄹ까 봐 after a vowel or -을까 봐 after a consonant
Use -았/었을까 봐 if the worry is about something past
State the action you took in the main clause
beginnerExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ까 봐 is the phrase Koreans use when worry drives an action, roughly worried that or afraid that. The structure is worry first, action second: 지각할까 봐 택시 탔어요 means I took a taxi because I was afraid I'd be late, and 비 올까 봐 우산 챙겼어요 means I packed an umbrella in case it rains. Attachment is the usual split, -ㄹ까 봐 after a vowel and -을까 봐 after a consonant, so 늦다 becomes 늦을까 봐. The key feeling is anxiety about a bad result, which is what separates it from the neutral reason marker -(으)니까; you would not use 배고플까 봐 just to say you're hungry. In casual texting you'll see the short 봐, but 봐요 sounds more polite when you talk to someone senior.

title: It seems / I think
plainEnglish: It softens a statement into a guess or impression, like English it seems or I think.
whenToUse: Use it to give a soft opinion or a guess instead of a flat assertion. Example: 그 식당 오늘 문 닫은 것 같아요 (That restaurant seems to be closed today).
attachmentRule: For a present verb add -는 것 같다 (가다→가는 것 같다, 먹다→먹는 것 같다). For a present adjective add -은 것 같다 after a consonant and -ㄴ 것 같다 after a vowel (춥다→추운 것 같다, 크다→큰 것 같다). Past uses the -(으)ㄴ modifier (간 것 같다, 먹은 것 같다) and future uses -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 (갈 것 같다). 것 is often spoken as 거, giving 가는 거 같아요.
contrastWith: -는 것 같다 is a soft personal guess, while -겠- and -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 lean toward prediction; Koreans use -는 것 같다 constantly to sound modest rather than too certain.

examples.ko: 이 카페 사람이 너무 많은 것 같아요.
examples.en: This cafe seems to have too many people.

examples.ko: 걔 요즘 좀 바쁜 것 같아.
examples.en: She seems kind of busy these days.
I think the delivery is going to be a bit late.

examples.ko: 어제 비 온 것 같아요. 길이 다 젖었어요.
examples.en: It seems it rained yesterday. The roads are all wet.

commonMistakes: Using the verb ending -는 것 같다 on an adjective, like 바쁘는 것 같다; adjectives take -은/-ㄴ 것 같다, so 바쁜 것 같다.
Confusing the tense modifier: 가는 것 같다 is present (seems to go), but 간 것 같다 is past (seems to have gone).

practiceItems.prompt: It seems like it's going to rain. (future)

studyOrder: Decide if the word is a verb or an adjective
Pick the tense: present, past -(으)ㄴ, or future -(으)ㄹ
Build the right modifier, e.g. 가는 / 간 / 갈
Add 것 같다 (or spoken 거 같아요) to mean it seems
beginnerExplanation: A/V-는 것 같다 is the everyday way Koreans soften what they say into a guess, like it seems or I think. It is everywhere in real conversation because stating things too bluntly can sound arrogant, so 그 식당 닫은 것 같아요 (it seems the place is closed) feels more natural than a flat assertion. The form rides on Korean's modifier endings: present verbs use -는 것 같다 (가는 것 같다), present adjectives use -은/-ㄴ 것 같다 (바쁜 것 같다), the past uses -(으)ㄴ 것 같다 (간 것 같다), and the future uses -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 (올 것 같다). In speech 것 almost always shrinks to 거, so you'll hear 가는 거 같아요. Two pitfalls: do not put the verb ending -는 on an adjective, and watch the tense modifier, since 가는 것 같다 and 간 것 같다 mean different things.

title: Decide to / agree to
plainEnglish: It says you decided or agreed to do something, often a plan with yourself or others.
whenToUse: Use it to announce a decision or a mutual plan. Example: 우리 다음 주에 만나기로 했어요 (We decided to meet next week).
attachmentRule: Attach -기로 하다 to the plain verb stem with no vowel or consonant change at all (가다→가기로 하다, 먹다→먹기로 하다, 운동하다→운동하기로 하다). The decision is usually reported in the past as -기로 했어요 (decided), since the choice is already made. To express a firm resolution you can say -기로 마음먹었어요. Negative is -지 않기로 하다 (안 가기로 했어요).
contrastWith: -기로 하다 marks a settled decision or agreement, while -(으)ㄹ게요 is an on-the-spot promise to the listener; use -기로 했어요 to report a plan you already locked in.

examples.en: I decided to quit smoking starting this year.
We decided to meet at the Han River this weekend.

examples.ko: 돈 모으려고 당분간 택시 안 타기로 했어.
examples.en: To save money, I decided not to take taxis for a while.
We decided to have a meeting with the team every Friday.

commonMistakes: Conjugating the verb before -기로, like 가아기로 하다; always use the plain stem, so 가기로 하다.
Using the present 하다 when the decision is already settled; a finished decision is normally -기로 했어요, not -기로 해요.

practiceItems.prompt: We decided to meet next week.

studyOrder: Identify the action you decided on
Take the plain verb stem with no change
Add -기로 하다, usually as -기로 했어요
For a negative decision use -지 않기로 or 안 ...-기로
beginnerExplanation: V-기로 하다 is how you announce a decision or a plan you've agreed on, and it is pleasantly regular because you just add -기로 하다 to the bare verb stem, no spelling changes. Because a decision is normally already made by the time you mention it, the natural form is the past -기로 했어요, so 우리 다음 주에 만나기로 했어요 means we decided to meet next week and 담배 끊기로 했어요 means I decided to quit smoking. It works for solo resolutions and for group agreements equally well. For a decision not to do something, slot in the negative: 안 가기로 했어요 or 가지 않기로 했어요. Keep it apart from -(으)ㄹ게요, which is a promise you make to someone right now; -기로 했어요 reports a plan you already settled.

title: Pretend to / act like
plainEnglish: It says someone pretends or fakes doing or being something.
whenToUse: Use it when a person acts a certain way without it being true. Example: 상사 와서 일하는 척했어요 (My boss came so I pretended to work).
attachmentRule: For a present verb add -는 척하다 (자다→자는 척하다, 먹다→먹는 척하다). For an adjective add -은 척하다 after a consonant and -ㄴ 척하다 after a vowel (아프다→아픈 척하다, 바쁘다→바쁜 척하다). Past action uses the -(으)ㄴ modifier (안 들은 척하다 = pretend not to have heard). You may also see 체하다, which means the same thing.
contrastWith: -는 척하다 means faking something that is not real, while -는 것 같다 means it genuinely seems true to you; the first is deliberate pretense, the second is an honest guess.

examples.en: My boss came so I pretended to be working hard.

examples.ko: 전 남친 마주쳤는데 그냥 못 본 척했어.
examples.en: I ran into my ex but I just pretended not to see him.
I pretended to be sick to skip the company dinner.
She totally knows but acts like she doesn't, you know.

commonMistakes: Using the verb ending -는 척하다 on an adjective, like 아프는 척하다; adjectives take -은/-ㄴ 척하다, so 아픈 척하다.
Confusing it with -는 것 같다: 자는 척하다 means pretending to sleep, but 자는 것 같다 means it seems she is sleeping.

practiceItems.prompt: I pretended not to hear. (past action)

studyOrder: Decide if the pretense is a verb or an adjective
Verbs: present -는 척, past action -(으)ㄴ 척
Adjectives: -은 척 after a consonant, -ㄴ 척 after a vowel
Add 척하다 and conjugate it for your tense
beginnerExplanation: V-는 척하다 means to pretend or fake, and it shows up a lot in stories about work, dating, and saving face. The form uses Korean's modifier endings: a present verb takes -는 척하다 (자는 척하다 = pretend to sleep, 일하는 척하다 = pretend to work), an adjective takes -은/-ㄴ 척하다 (아픈 척하다 = pretend to be sick), and a past action takes -(으)ㄴ 척하다, as in 못 본 척했어 (pretended not to see). A super common real-life line is 상사 와서 일하는 척했어요, which any office worker will recognize. The classic mistake is treating it like -는 것 같다; but those are opposites in spirit, since 척하다 is deliberate faking while 것 같다 is an honest impression, so 자는 척하다 (pretending to sleep) is very different from 자는 것 같다 (seems to be sleeping).
